title: Voltage, current, resistance & Ohm's law
intro: Electricity becomes easier to understand when you separate electrical pressure (voltage), flow (current) and opposition (resistance). Calculate first, then connect a circuit.
learn: Distinguish volts (V), amperes (A) and ohms (Ω).
Use I = V/R and P = V×I on a DC circuit.
Explain why an LED needs a current-limiting resistor.
concepts: Voltage (V)
The difference in electrical potential between two nodes; it provides the push for current.
Current (I)
How quickly electrical charge moves through a closed circuit; measured in amperes.
Resistance (R)
Opposition to current, measured in ohms. For an ideal resistor, V = I×R.
Power (P)
Rate of electrical energy transfer: P = V×I, measured in watts.
diagram:
5 V DC + ──[ 330 Ω resistor ]──|>|── GND
                              LED

Approximate red LED drop = 2 V
I = (5 V − 2 V) / 330 Ω ≈ 0.009 A (9 mA)
steps: Before wiring, calculate the LED current: (5 − 2)/330 ≈ 9 mA.
Use a suitable regulated low-voltage 5 V supply; disconnect power before adding parts.
Connect resistor and LED in series, observing LED polarity.
Power on and compare the LED brightness with your expected result.
outcome: A closed current-limited path lights the LED. If the LED is reversed, it normally stays off.
challenge: Recalculate the current using 220 Ω instead of 330 Ω. Which choice causes more current?
question: Why is the resistor connected in series with the LED?
answer: It limits current. An LED does not self-limit current safely when connected directly to 5 V.
safety: Use only a low-voltage, current-limited DC source. Do not connect electronic parts to mains power.
references: SparkFun: Voltage, current, resistance and Ohm's law

title: Recognize components & schematic symbols
intro: A schematic is a map of electrical connections—not a photograph. Learn to identify what common parts do before trying to build from a diagram.
learn: Identify resistors, capacitors, diodes, LEDs, transistors and switches.
Recognize polarity-sensitive components.
Read how a symbol corresponds to a physical part.
concepts: Resistor
Limits current and creates voltage drops. A schematic often uses a rectangle or zigzag.
Capacitor
Stores charge; nonpolar ceramics and polarized electrolytics require different handling.
Diode / LED
Conducts preferentially in one direction; an LED also emits light.
Transistor
Controls a larger load current using an input signal; confirm model and pinout.
diagram:
Resistor      ──[ R ]──
Capacitor     ──| |──
Diode         ──|>|──
LED           ──|>|──  ↗↗
Open switch   ──o/ o──
Ground           ⏚

Symbols show connections, not physical dimensions.
steps: Lay out the six parts in front of you without power.
Identify the printed value, part number, or polarity mark on each.
Sketch the symbols and write the physical pin names beside them.
For a diode, find the cathode stripe; for an electrolytic capacitor, find the negative stripe.
Check a specific transistor datasheet before assigning emitter, base and collector pins.
outcome: You should be able to match a component and its symbol and explain whether orientation matters.
challenge: Sketch a circuit consisting of a battery, resistor, switch and LED connected in a single loop.
question: Which listed capacitor is generally polarized: ceramic or aluminum electrolytic?
answer: Aluminum electrolytic capacitors are normally polarized; common ceramic capacitors are usually nonpolarized.
safety: Never reverse a polarized electrolytic capacitor or exceed its marked voltage.

title: Breadboard rows, rails & common ground
intro: A solderless breadboard hides metal spring connections underneath its holes. Understanding the internal connections prevents many first-time wiring mistakes.
learn: Distinguish terminal strips from power rails.
Use a shared ground reference.
Avoid accidentally bridging power and ground.
concepts: Terminal strips
On a typical breadboard, groups of five holes on each side of the central channel are internally linked.
Power rails
Long side rails often distribute supply and ground, but some boards have split rails.
Common ground
Two modules need a shared reference when exchanging non-isolated electrical signals.
diagram:
Typical center gap layout (viewed from top)

    a b c d e   |   f g h i j
row1 ●─●─●─●─●  |  ●─●─●─●─● row1
row2 ●─●─●─●─●  |  ●─●─●─●─● row2
                 gap
Each horizontal group of 5 connects together.
Side rails may be continuous OR split—test them.
steps: Disconnect any power source.
Pick one row and insert a resistor across two DIFFERENT connected groups.
Use a continuity meter, if available, to test linked holes.
Identify any break in the side power rails.
Label the intended positive and ground rails; check again before powering.
outcome: You can trace every connection on the breadboard without guessing from wire colors.
challenge: Explain why both resistor legs inserted into the same five-hole group cannot add series resistance to a circuit.
question: Are all holes in one horizontal row on opposite sides of the center gap connected?
answer: No. The center channel isolates the two five-hole groups in the common breadboard layout.
safety: Never assume the side rails are continuous across the entire board; confirm with a multimeter.

title: Series vs. parallel circuits
intro: Connections determine whether components share the same current or the same voltage. This concept explains everything from LEDs to battery wiring.
learn: Calculate equivalent resistance for simple series circuits.
Identify parallel branches.
Explain why LEDs in parallel generally need separate resistors.
concepts: Series
One path: same current passes through all series elements. R_total = R1 + R2.
Parallel
Multiple branches: each branch has the same voltage. 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2.
Safe LED branches
Each parallel LED branch should normally have its own current-limiting resistor.
steps: On paper, draw two resistors end-to-end (series).
Calculate R_total = 330 + 330 = 660 Ω.
Draw the same two resistors between the same pair of nodes (parallel).
If using a meter, disconnect power and compare both measured resistances.
outcome: You can tell from the connection diagram which quantities add and which remain equal.
challenge: What is the equivalent resistance of 220 Ω and 330 Ω in series?
question: In a parallel network, what electrical quantity is the same across each branch?
answer: Voltage is the same between the common pair of parallel nodes.
safety: Measure resistance only with power disconnected; never put a meter in ohms mode across an energized circuit.

title: Build your first resistor–LED circuit
intro: This no-code circuit demonstrates polarity, a closed loop and current limiting. It is a good first build before using a microcontroller.
learn: Select a series resistor.
Read LED polarity.
Troubleshoot an open circuit.
concepts: Resistor sizing
For a red LED at roughly 2 V on a 5 V supply, a 330 Ω resistor gives approximately 9 mA.
LED polarity
Long lead typically anode (+); short lead / flat edge typically cathode (−).
steps: Unplug the supply and insert the LED across separate breadboard rows.
Connect 330 Ω between 5 V positive and the LED anode.
Connect the cathode to GND; keep the positive and negative rails apart.
Apply regulated 5 V, then inspect the light.
Unplug power before trying a different resistor.
outcome: The red LED lights steadily. If not, check the polarity, resistor placement and shared row connections.
challenge: Swap 330 Ω for 470 Ω and predict the change in brightness.
question: What happens if you omit the current-limiting resistor?
answer: The LED may draw excessive current and fail; keep a suitable series resistor.
safety: Never connect an LED directly across a 5 V power source without a correctly sized resistor.

title: Make a reliable pushbutton input
intro: A switch opens and closes a connection. Without a pull-up or pull-down, the input can float and behave unpredictably.
learn: Explain floating inputs.
Use the Arduino's internal pull-up resistor.
Understand why a pressed button reads LOW.
concepts: Floating input
An unconnected input is neither guaranteed HIGH nor LOW.
INPUT_PULLUP
Enables a built-in resistor that keeps the input HIGH until a switch connects it to GND.
diagram:
Arduino UNO D2 ────o  o──── GND
                    pushbutton

pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP)
Not pressed = HIGH
Pressed     = LOW
steps: With USB disconnected, place the button across the center breadboard gap.
Check the button's internal paired terminals; use opposite contacts that close when pressed.
Connect one switch contact to Uno D2 and the other to GND.
Open the corresponding Arduino coding lesson below and upload the button sketch.
Watch the Serial Monitor or connected LED as you press and release.
outcome: The digital input rests HIGH and changes to LOW while the button is held.
challenge: Why does a button wired to GND read LOW when pressed rather than HIGH?
question: What does INPUT_PULLUP prevent?
answer: It prevents the input from floating when the switch is open.
safety: Do not connect a pin configured INPUT_PULLUP to an external voltage above the board's logic level.
references: Arduino: Built-in input and button examples

title: Potentiometer as a voltage divider
intro: A three-terminal potentiometer can vary a voltage between the ends of its supply. This is the starting point for analog controls.
learn: Identify the wiper (middle terminal).
Wire a potentiometer between 5 V and GND.
Understand how voltage maps to Arduino analog readings.
concepts: Voltage divider
The wiper picks a fraction of the supply voltage when the end terminals are connected between supply and ground.
Analog input
On the Uno R3 the default 10-bit ADC reads approximately 0–1023 over the reference-voltage range.
diagram:
Uno 5 V ──── pot outer terminal
                 │
                 ├── wiper (middle) ── Uno A0
                 │
Uno GND ──── pot other outer terminal
steps: Disconnect USB power before wiring.
Connect one outer terminal to 5 V and the other to GND.
Connect the middle/wiper terminal to A0.
Upload the analog-input lesson sketch and open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud.
Turn the shaft gradually and observe numbers changing from near 0 to near 1023.
outcome: The wiper voltage changes smoothly, and the serial readings follow its position.
challenge: If the ADC shows 512, estimate the wiper voltage on a 5 V Uno using 512/1023 × 5.
question: What happens if the wiper wire is left disconnected?
answer: A0 floats; readings can become erratic and no longer reliably represent the knob position.
safety: Use the board's 5 V reference only on a 5 V Uno. Never put 5 V directly into a 3.3 V-only ESP32 analog pin.

title: Switch a 5 V buzzer with a transistor
intro: A transistor lets a tiny digital control signal turn a larger low-voltage load on or off. Build a practical NPN low-side switch.
learn: Identify base, collector and emitter from a datasheet.
Use a base resistor and a shared ground.
Explain why the Arduino pin does not directly power a high-current load.
concepts: NPN low-side switch
The emitter connects to GND; the collector sinks current from a load connected to +5 V.
Base resistor
Limits the current driven into the transistor base.
Load rating
The transistor must safely handle the actual buzzer current; choose an external driver for larger loads.
diagram:
5 V ──[active buzzer + ]
        [active buzzer − ]──── C   NPN (2N2222*)
                              │
Uno D8 ──[1 kΩ]────────────── B
                              E ─── GND
Uno GND ─────────────────────────── GND
*Verify exact E-B-C pin order using the transistor datasheet.
steps: Verify the specific transistor's E/B/C pinout before inserting it.
Ensure the active buzzer's current is within the transistor and power source limits.
Wire emitter to ground and collector to the buzzer's negative lead.
Connect the buzzer positive lead to regulated +5 V.
Connect Uno D8 to base through 1 kΩ, then upload the sketch.
Confirm a one-second beep followed by a one-second pause.
codeNotes: HIGH on D8 supplies a small base current, saturating the NPN switch if properly sized.
The buzzer current flows through the load and transistor, not directly through D8.
outcome: The active buzzer sounds once per second when the transistor is driven on.
challenge: Why does this circuit need the Uno GND connected to the transistor emitter ground?
question: Can an Arduino digital output safely drive any motor or relay coil directly?
answer: No. Loads must stay within pin-current limits; use a correctly rated driver, supply and flyback diode for inductive loads.
safety: Use only a low-voltage active buzzer with a known current rating. Verify transistor pinout and driver dissipation; do not switch mains.

title: Install Arduino IDE & upload your first sketch
intro: An Arduino sketch is a C++ program compiled for your board. Start with the built-in LED so you can prove your software and USB connection work before wiring any components.
learn: Install the official Arduino IDE.
Select the correct board and serial port.
Recognize setup(), loop(), pinMode() and digitalWrite().
concepts: setup()
Runs once after reset or power-on; initialize pins and serial communication here.
loop()
Runs repeatedly until power is removed or the board resets.
digitalWrite()
Writes HIGH or LOW to an output pin.
diagram:
Computer ──USB data cable──> Uno R3
                              │
                        LED_BUILTIN (D13)
                        No external LED required
parts: Arduino Uno R3 USB Type-C compatible
steps: Install Arduino IDE from arduino.cc/en/software.
Connect the Uno using a data-capable USB cable; install the appropriate clone USB driver only if needed.
Under Tools → Board, select Arduino Uno; select the detected Port.
Paste the sketch below, then click Verify (✓).
Click Upload (→) and watch the built-in LED blink once each second.
codeNotes: LED_BUILTIN refers to the built-in LED pin for the selected board.
delay(1000) pauses the sketch for 1000 milliseconds (one second).
outcome: The onboard LED blinks: one second on, one second off.
challenge: Change both 1000 delays to 250; verify that the blinking becomes faster.
question: Which function runs repeatedly while the Arduino is operating?
answer: loop() runs repeatedly. setup() runs once after reset or startup.
safety: Start with only the USB-connected Uno; no external wiring is needed.

title: Variables, constants & digital outputs
intro: Learn how the compiler stores a pin number and how a small reusable function can control an external LED.
learn: Use const byte for a pin number.
Create a simple helper function.
Control an external LED through a resistor.
concepts: const byte
Stores a small constant pin number without allowing accidental reassignment.
Function
A named section of reusable code.
HIGH / LOW
Two digital logic states. On a 5 V Uno, HIGH is a logic-level output near 5 V.
diagram:
Uno D9 ──[330 Ω]── LED anode (+)
                     |>| LED
Uno GND ────────── LED cathode (−)
steps: With USB disconnected, build the resistor-LED circuit.
Select Arduino Uno and the correct USB serial port.
Paste and upload the sketch.
Observe a short blink followed by a longer pause.
Modify shortFlash(200) to shortFlash(500) and upload again.
codeNotes: ledPin is a readable name for hardware pin D9.
shortFlash() accepts the on-duration as a parameter, making code easier to reuse.
outcome: The external LED lights for 200 ms then stays off for 800 ms.
challenge: Create three flashes by calling shortFlash(100) three times with 100 ms pauses.
question: Why is const byte ledPin = 9 better than writing 9 everywhere?
answer: It makes the meaning clear and lets you change the pin in just one place.
safety: Use a resistor with the LED and avoid drawing excessive current from the microcontroller pin.

title: Read a button with if/else
intro: A digital input allows code to respond to the world. Use INPUT_PULLUP and a button between D2 and GND, then drive an LED.
learn: Configure a digital input with INPUT_PULLUP.
Read a pin with digitalRead().
Make a decision with if/else.
concepts: digitalRead()
Returns HIGH or LOW from a digital pin.
if/else
Executes different code based on a true/false condition.
Active low
With INPUT_PULLUP a pressed button reads LOW.
diagram:
BUTTON: Uno D2 ──o  o── GND

LED:    Uno D9 ──[330 Ω]──|>|── GND
steps: Disconnect USB before wiring the pushbutton and resistor/LED.
Place the switch across the breadboard center gap; verify its contact pairs.
Build the two connections shown in the diagram.
Upload the sketch below.
Press and release the button to see the LED follow the input.
codeNotes: digitalRead(buttonPin) == LOW becomes true when pressing the button.
With no time-based delays, the LED changes quickly when the button state changes.
outcome: The LED stays off until the button is pressed; it lights while held.
challenge: Reverse the behavior: LED on when released, off when pressed.
question: Why is the condition == LOW rather than == HIGH?
answer: The button pulls D2 to ground when pressed; the internal pull-up keeps D2 HIGH otherwise.
safety: Confirm pushbutton pin pairs; incorrectly wiring 5 V straight to GND could short the supply.

title: Read analog values & use Serial Monitor
intro: The Uno converts analog voltage into a digital number. A potentiometer on A0 gives you a simple way to see analog-to-digital conversion in practice.
learn: Connect a 10 kΩ potentiometer as a divider.
Use analogRead(A0) and Serial.println().
Convert a 10-bit ADC reading into an approximate voltage.
concepts: ADC
Analog-to-digital converter: reads a voltage and produces a number.
Serial Monitor
Displays text data over USB to help debug a running program.
Conversion
For a default 5 V Uno reference: volts ≈ reading × (5.0/1023.0).
diagram:
5 V ── pot outer A
        |
A0 ─── wiper (middle)
        |
GND ── pot outer B

USB Serial Monitor baud = 9600
steps: Disconnect USB and connect the three potentiometer terminals.
Upload the sketch.
Open Tools → Serial Monitor and set the baud to 9600.
Rotate the knob and inspect the reading and estimated voltage.
Remove A0 from the wiper briefly to notice why floating analog inputs are unreliable, then reconnect with power off.
codeNotes: Serial.begin(9600) initializes the USB serial text connection.
analogRead(A0) returns about 0 at 0 V and 1023 near the Uno's reference voltage.
outcome: As you turn the knob, the serial values move smoothly across the ADC range.
challenge: Create a warning message when raw is greater than 800.
question: Why must Serial Monitor use the same baud as Serial.begin()?
answer: Matching baud rates are required for the serial data to be decoded correctly.
safety: The voltage conversion assumes the default 5 V reference; actual USB supply can vary. Never apply more than the reference/supply limit to an input.

title: PWM fading: control LED brightness
intro: Pulse-width modulation (PWM) switches an output rapidly on and off. The duty cycle changes average power, letting an LED appear dimmer or brighter.
learn: Identify PWM-capable pins on an Uno.
Use analogWrite() to set an 8-bit duty cycle.
Write a for loop for a gradual fade.
concepts: PWM duty cycle
The fraction of time a signal is HIGH during each cycle.
analogWrite()
On an Uno PWM pin, values 0–255 set an 8-bit PWM duty cycle; this is not a true analog DC voltage.
for loop
Repeats a block while changing a counter.
diagram:
Uno PWM D9 ──[330 Ω]──|>|── GND
                         LED

analogWrite(9, 0)   ≈ 0% on
analogWrite(9, 128) ≈ 50% on
analogWrite(9, 255) ≈ 100% on
steps: Build the resistor/LED connection with power off.
Upload the fading sketch.
Observe the light grow brighter then dimmer.
Change the step size from 5 to 10 to see how the fade changes.
Try another PWM-capable Uno pin, updating the constant in the code.
codeNotes: PWM output changes the ratio of ON time to OFF time, not the pin's voltage ceiling.
A resistor is still required to protect the LED.
outcome: The LED fades up and down repeatedly.
challenge: Make the fade slower by doubling delay(25) to delay(50).
question: Does analogWrite(9, 128) create a steady 2.5 V DC output on an Uno?
answer: No. It normally produces a digital PWM waveform with about a 50% duty cycle.
safety: Do not connect high-power LEDs or motors directly to an Uno digital pin.

title: Non-blocking timers with millis()
intro: delay() stops your sketch from doing other work. millis() helps schedule multiple events without waiting inside each event.
learn: Read the number of milliseconds since boot.
Compare elapsed time using unsigned long subtraction.
Run two different blink intervals simultaneously.
concepts: millis()
Returns elapsed milliseconds as an unsigned long; rolls over after approximately 49.7 days on common 32-bit Arduino platforms.
Elapsed-time check
Use now - previous >= interval to handle timer rollover correctly.
Non-blocking
Other code can continue running while waiting for the next event.
diagram:
Uno D8 ──[330 Ω]──|>|── GND (LED A)
Uno D9 ──[330 Ω]──|>|── GND (LED B)

LED A: toggle every 500 ms
LED B: toggle every 750 ms
No delay() calls.
steps: Disconnect power and wire two individually resisted LEDs.
Upload the sketch.
Observe two different blink rates without long pauses.
Add Serial.println(now) inside loop() temporarily to observe that the loop keeps running.
Change the second interval to 250 ms and upload again.
codeNotes: Each LED has its own timestamp and interval, so its schedule is independent.
Unsigned subtraction allows these interval comparisons to work across millis() rollover.
outcome: The two LEDs flash at different intervals while the main loop stays responsive.
challenge: Add a pushbutton input that can be read immediately without being blocked by delays.
question: Why do we use now - lastA rather than now >= lastA + intervalA?
answer: Unsigned subtraction handles timer wraparound more reliably and avoids overflow in addition-based comparisons.
safety: Use one resistor per LED and test button additions with power disconnected.
